title_en: 成都市人民检察院诉尚荣多等人贪污案
keywords_en: Criminal; Embezzlement; First Instance; Intermediate People's Court; Sichuan Province; Natural Person; State Organ; Criminal Law; Whether the discretionary admission fee constitutes public property; Whether intercepting and privately distributing the discretionary admission fee constitutes the crime of embezzlement; Support the plaintiff; Admission work; Discretionary admission fee; Interception of public funds; Private distribution of public funds
full_text_en:
Chengdu People's Procuratorate v. Shang Rongduo et al. — corruption

[Ruling Summary]

Where a staff member of a state-owned institution takes advantage of his position to intercept and embezzle unreasonable fees illegally collected by his unit, he shall be convicted of corruption in accordance with Article 382 of the Criminal Law of the PRC.

Procuratorial Authority: Chengdu People's Procuratorate, Sichuan Province.

Defendant: Shang Rongduo, male, 47 years old, Vice President of Chengdu University of Technology. Arrested on June 29, 2003.

Defendant: Li Yuming, male, 43 years old, Vice Dean of the College of Communication and Art, Chengdu University of Technology. Arrested on June 12, 2003.

The Chengdu People's Procuratorate instituted a public prosecution against the defendants Shang Rongduo and Li Yuming for corruption before the Chengdu Intermediate People's Court.

The indictment alleged: During the 2001 enrollment work of the former Sichuan Commercial College (hereinafter referred to as the College), defendants Shang Rongduo, in his capacity as Vice President of the College, and Li Yuming, then Deputy Secretary of the Party Committee of the College, were in charge of the enrollment leading group. They, together with Peng Yibin, Director of the Student Affairs Office of the College (separately dealt with), conspired to embezzle RMB 200,000 from the "discretionary admission fees" collected during this enrollment, with Shang Rongduo receiving illicit gains of RMB 50,000, Li Yuming receiving RMB 60,000, and Peng Yibin receiving RMB 40,000. After the enrollment work concluded, Shang Rongduo instructed Peng Yibin to transfer RMB 50,000 from the "discretionary admission fees" that had been handed over to the College but then fully withdrawn back, into Shang Rongduo's personal account. Shang Rongduo withdrew this sum in two installments for personal expenses. The conduct of Shang Rongduo and Li Yuming violated the provisions of Article 382 of the Criminal Law of the PRC (hereinafter referred to as the Criminal Law), constituting the crime of corruption. In the joint corruption, Shang Rongduo was the principal offender, and Li Yuming was an accessory. Li Yuming displayed a good attitude in admitting guilt and showed repentance, which could warrant a lighter punishment at the court's discretion. Please impose criminal liability on the two persons according to law.

Defendant Shang Rongduo denied committing the crime of corruption, arguing that his confession during the investigation was not true, that the enrollment leading group had the authority to dispose of the "discretionary admission fees", that the un-surrendered "discretionary admission fees" were intended to reward those who made significant contributions to enrollment, and that the RMB 50,000 he withdrew was used to pay New Year visits to leaders of relevant units.

Shang Rongduo's defense counsel argued that Shang Rongduo and the other two, as the principal persons in charge of enrollment, should have been heavily rewarded in accordance with the college committee's reward policy, which had precedent in the Adult Education Department of the College; that the purpose of Shang Rongduo and others withdrawing RMB 200,000 from the "discretionary admission fees" was to heavily reward those who contributed to the enrollment office, which was an authorized act of duty by the college committee; that the RMB 50,000 withdrawn by Shang Rongduo was also used for enrollment work, specifically for paying New Year visits to relevant persons in the education commission and other departments. Although these persons denied receiving money, the credibility of their testimony was questionable. In sum, Shang Rongduo's conduct did not constitute corruption.

Defendant Li Yuming argued that the "discretionary admission fees" were retained according to customary practice and distributed to individuals based on their contributions. He was in a passive position throughout the matter and should not be convicted of corruption.

Li Yuming's defense counsel argued that the state had regulations prohibiting the collection of "discretionary admission fees", therefore such fees could not be considered state property. The school illegally collected "discretionary admission fees" and even formulated a policy of "using enrollment fees to support enrollment" and having the enrollment leading group specifically handle rewards for the use of these fees. Therefore, the distribution of "discretionary admission fees" as bonuses by Li Yuming and others did not infringe upon the ownership of state property; it only infringed upon the private property rights of the students' parents, which was a civil tort issue. The indictment charging Li Yuming with corruption lacked factual and legal basis. Given that Li Yuming was in a subordinate position in this case and voluntarily returned his share of RMB 60,000 after the investigation authority became involved, if his conduct constituted a crime, he should be given a lighter punishment.

The Chengdu Intermediate People's Court found through trial:

(I) During the 2001 enrollment work of the former College, defendants Shang Rongduo and Li Yuming were in charge of the enrollment admission leading group, and Peng Yibin, Director of the Student Affairs Office, was specifically responsible for collecting and keeping the "discretionary admission fees". After the enrollment work concluded in October 2001, the three persons, Shang Rongduo, Li Yuming, and Peng Yibin, conducted a count and found that, after deducting expenses for enrollment work, the remaining balance of the "discretionary admission fees" was RMB 342,000. After discussion, the three decided to surrender only RMB 142,000 to the College. On November 28, 2001, Peng Yibin transferred RMB 200,000 into a personal account opened in his son's name. Before the Spring Festival of 2002, Shang Rongduo, Li Yuming, and Peng Yibin conspired to divide the intercepted RMB 200,000 among themselves, agreeing that each of the three would receive RMB 60,000 and that Zhang Xiaonan, the former President of the College, would receive RMB 20,000. Later, Shang Rongduo separately approached Peng Yibin and decided: Li Yuming would still receive RMB 60,000, Shang Rongduo would receive RMB 50,000, Peng Yibin would receive RMB 40,000, and Zhang Xiaonan would receive RMB 50,000. Subsequently, Peng Yibin gave Li Yuming RMB 60,000, deposited RMB 50,000 into Shang Rongduo's personal account, and gave Zhang Xiaonan RMB 50,000 under the pretext of activity funds retained by the Student Affairs Office; however, Zhang Xiaonan returned the money at that time.

The following evidence confirms the above facts:

1. Confession of Shang Rongduo. Main content: The members of the school enrollment leading group included himself, Li Yuming, and Peng Yibin, and he was in charge. After the 2001 enrollment work ended, the three persons checked the "discretionary admission fees" collected that year. After deducting already disbursed items such as reward fees and activity fees, over RMB 300,000 remained. At that time, the three agreed to withdraw RMB 200,000 to distribute and surrender over RMB 140,000 to the school. Regarding how to distribute the RMB 200,000, the three initially agreed that each person would get RMB 60,000. Later, he separately approached Peng Yibin and decided to give President Zhang Xiaonan RMB 50,000. Peng Yibin gave Li Yuming RMB 60,000, gave him RMB 50,000, and Zhang Xiaonan did not take the money. No one except himself, Li Yuming, and Peng Yibin knew about the RMB 200,000. In May 2003, the three discussed that if the University of Technology inquired about the "discretionary admission fees", they should say that only over RMB 140,000 was collected; if a higher authority investigated, they should say that over RMB 400,000 was collected, with over RMB 100,000 used for rewards, over RMB 100,000 used for activity fees, over RMB 140,000 surrendered to the school, and each of them took RMB 20,000 as reward fees.

2. Confession of Li Yuming. Main content: The College began collecting "discretionary admission fees" in 1999, issuing receipts that year. In 2000 and 2001, no receipts were issued. Each year, the fees were collected by Peng Yibin, Director of the Student Affairs Office, who deposited part in the bank and used part for enrollment expenses. After each year's enrollment work ended, Peng Yibin reported the fee collection and expenses to Shang Rongduo and himself, and then Shang Rongduo reported to the school. Shang Rongduo had the authority to decide on activity fees and reward fees for enrollment personnel, but should report to the school. After deducting expenses, the remaining "discretionary admission fees" should be surrendered to the school's finance office. The total "discretionary admission fees" collected in 2001 were over RMB 400,000. No one else knew about the three intercepting RMB 200,000. In early February 2002, the three agreed to divide the RMB 200,000 privately, each getting RMB 60,000, and Zhang Xiaonan getting RMB 20,000. Around February 6 or 7, 2002, Peng Yibin gave him the money. On the evening of February 25, 2003, he, Shang Rongduo, and Peng Yibin discussed how to present a consistent story, agreeing that no one should mention the private distribution of the RMB 200,000.

3. Testimony of witness Peng Yibin. Main content: In 2001, the College admitted approximately over 200 students through discretionary admission, with approximately 140-150 students actually paying fees, totaling over RMB 540,000 in fees collected. After the enrollment ended, he reported the total fees collected and the student roster to Shang Rongduo and Li Yuming. The three agreed to withdraw RMB 200,000 from the "discretionary admission fees" for separate safekeeping and surrender only RMB 142,000 to the school's finance office. Before the Spring Festival of 2002, the three discussed each getting RMB 60,000, with the remaining RMB 20,000 for Zhang Xiaonan. Later, Shang Rongduo discussed with him again, deciding that Shang Rongduo and Zhang Xiaonan would each get RMB 50,000 and he would get RMB 40,000. He transferred RMB 50,000 to Shang Rongduo from his account, withdrew RMB 60,000 in cash and gave it to Li Yuming, and gave RMB 50,000 to Zhang Xiaonan, but Zhang returned the money. Only the three of them knew about the interception of the RMB 200,000.

4. Testimony of witness Zhang Xiaonan. Main content: The College had regulations prohibiting concealing the "discretionary admission fees" collected. At the end of 2001, Shang Rongduo said that the "discretionary admission fees" amounted to nearly RMB 400,000, with RMB 140,000 surrendered to the school's finance office, over RMB 100,000 used for enrollment activity expenses, and the remaining money distributed to everyone as enrollment reward fees. He agreed to reward all enrollment personnel according to usual practice. Shang Rongduo never told him about intercepting RMB 200,000 from the "discretionary admission fees". Before the Spring Festival of 2002, Peng Yibin gave him RMB 50,000, claiming it was expenses retained by the Student Affairs Office. He did not accept it and returned the money to Peng Yibin.

5. Testimony of witness Cai Yongheng. Main content: During his tenure as Vice President of the College, no one informed him about the collection and expenditure of the 2001 discretionary admission fees. Based on the division of responsibilities, this work was handled by Shang Rongduo.

6. Testimony of witness Xie Fei. Main content: During his tenure as Finance Director of the College, he did not know how much "discretionary admission fees" the Student Affairs Office collected each year. On October 22, 2001, Peng Yibin wanted to surrender the 2001 "discretionary admission fees" in the amount of RMB 142,000, and he agreed to keep it for him temporarily. A week later, Peng Yibin took the money back and reportedly surrendered it to the University of Technology.

7. Testimonies of over 70 witnesses, including Chen Wanlin, confirming that they each paid "discretionary admission fees" when admitted to the College in 2001.

8. Detailed account records of the personal accounts of Peng Yibin and Shang Rongduo, confirming that on December 28, 2001, Peng Yibin transferred RMB 200,000 into the account of his son Peng Jun; and in February 2001, RMB 50,000 was transferred from Peng Jun's account into Shang Rongduo's account.

(II) In December 2001, defendant Shang Rongduo asked Peng Yibin to withdraw some money from the RMB 142,000 in "discretionary admission fees" as activity funds. Peng Yibin wrote a report in the name of rewarding enrollment staff, which was approved by Cai Yongheng, Vice President responsible for administrative work at that time. Subsequently, RMB 57,000 was withdrawn from the "discretionary admission fees". Peng Yibin, following Shang Rongduo's instructions, used RMB 7,000 of this amount for bonuses in the Student Affairs Office and deposited RMB 50,000 into Shang Rongduo's personal account on December 28, 2001. Shang Rongduo withdrew this money in two installments on December 31, 2001, and January 4, 2002, respectively, for personal expenses.

The following evidence confirms the above facts:

1. Confession of defendant Shang Rongduo. Main content: According to school regulations, a certain amount of activity funds could be withdrawn each year based on the number of enrolled students. In 2001, he approved Peng Yibin's report to withdraw RMB 57,000 from the RMB 142,000 in "discretionary admission fees" to be surrendered to the University of Technology. They used RMB 7,000 for the Student Affairs Office and the remaining RMB 50,000, he used after the Spring Festival of 2002 to pay New Year visits to leaders of the Provincial Education Department and the Provincial Enrollment Office. This matter was not collectively studied, nor was it reported to school leaders.

2. Testimony of witness Peng Yibin. Main content: Around December 2001, he wrote a slip for withdrawing expenses in the amount of RMB 57,000 as instructed by Shang Rongduo, with the date noted as before October, before the merger of schools. Vice President Cai Yongheng signed it. At that time, RMB 7,000 was given to the Student Affairs Office as a reward. The remaining RMB 50,000, Shang Rongduo instructed him to deposit into Shang's personal account in December 2001. He did not know what Shang Rongduo used the RMB 50,000 for.

3. Testimony of witness Zhang Xiaonan. Main content: The College did not collectively discuss paying New Year visits to relevant units and individuals; from the second half of 2001 to 2002, the school had already been merged, so there was no situation of paying New Year visits. When Shang Rongduo reported the use of "discretionary admission fees", he did not mention using part of the funds for New Year visits.

4. Testimonies of witnesses Zhao Jiaping, Zhang Xiaoxia, Qian Renfang, Wu Yuelian, and Zou Mingyuan, all confirming that they had no financial dealings with defendant Shang Rongduo, and Shang Rongduo did not pay them New Year visits during the Spring Festival of 2002.

5. Testimonies of witnesses Hong Liu, Li Wanyin, Yang Congjian, Luo Shunlin, Xue Daohua, and Zhou Guoliang, all testifying that they did not know Shang Rongduo.

6. Testimonies of witness Zheng Jianqiang and his wife Fang Mei, confirming that in May-June 2003, Shang Rongduo approached them, saying he had some trouble with money, and asked them to help testify, if asked, that they had lent Shang Rongduo RMB 100,000 in February 2002, and Shang returned it in April 2003. In fact, they had not lent any money to Shang Rongduo.

7. Detailed account records of the personal accounts of Peng Yibin and Shang Rongduo, confirming that on December 28, 2001, Peng Yibin transferred RMB 50,000 out of the RMB 57,000 into Shang Rongduo's account.

The Chengdu Intermediate People's Court held:

Article 382 of the Criminal Law of the PRC provides: "Any functionary of a state organ who, by taking advantage of his position, misappropriates, steals, swindles or illegally takes by other means public property shall be guilty of corruption." Defendants Shang Rongduo and Li Yuming, as state functionaries engaged in public service in educational institutions, took advantage of their positions in charge of school enrollment work to jointly embezzle RMB 200,000 of public funds with Peng Yibin, and Shang Rongduo additionally embezzled RMB 50,000 personally. Their conduct constituted the crime of corruption. Shang Rongduo participated in the joint embezzlement of RMB 200,000 and personally embezzled RMB 50,000, with illegal gains of RMB 100,000. Shang Rongduo was the principal person in charge of the enrollment work and played a primary role in the joint corruption, thus being the principal offender. Li Yuming participated in the joint embezzlement of RMB 200,000, with illegal gains of RMB 60,000. Li Yuming played a supplementary role in the joint corruption, thus being an accessory. In accordance with Article 383 of the Criminal Law, both Shang Rongduo and Li Yuming should be sentenced to fixed-term imprisonment of not less than ten years or life imprisonment. Given that Shang Rongduo truthfully confessed to the basic criminal facts and the illicit gains have been recovered, a lighter punishment may be imposed at the court's discretion when sentencing; Li Yuming was an accessory, the illicit gains have been recovered, and he displayed a good attitude in admitting guilt, so a mitigated punishment may be imposed when sentencing. The charges brought by the indictment against the two defendants are established.

Defendant Shang Rongduo and his defense counsel argued that Shang Rongduo and others withdrew RMB 200,000 to heavily reward those who contributed to the enrollment office, which was a normal act of performing their duties; defendant Li Yuming's defense counsel argued that the school indeed had a reward policy. Upon investigation, the evidence in this case proves that the purpose of Shang Rongduo, Li Yuming, and Peng Yibin in conspiring to withdraw RMB 200,000 was to divide it among themselves privately, not to reward enrollment staff. Therefore, this defense argument by Shang Rongduo, Li Yuming, and their defense counsels is inconsistent with the facts and is not adopted.

Defendant Shang Rongduo and his defense counsel argued that the RMB 50,000 withdrawn by Shang Rongduo was used to pay New Year visits to leaders of relevant units and did not constitute corruption. Upon investigation, there is no evidence in this case proving that Shang Rongduo gave this money to relevant leaders in the name of the unit. As to how he personally used the money, that concerns the disposition of illicit gains and does not affect the nature of the illicit gains. This defense argument by Shang Rongduo and his defense counsel lacks evidentiary support and is not adopted.

Defendant Li Yuming's defense counsel's request for a lighter punishment for Li Yuming has factual and legal basis and should be adopted.

Accordingly, the Chengdu Intermediate People's Court rendered the following judgment on April 2, 2004:

1. Defendant Shang Rongduo is guilty of corruption and sentenced to fixed-term imprisonment of ten years.

2. Defendant Li Yuming is guilty of corruption and, with a mitigated sentence, sentenced to fixed-term imprisonment of six years.

3. The illegal gains of RMB 100,000 of defendant Shang Rongduo and the illegal gains of RMB 60,000 of defendant Li Yuming are to be recovered and turned over to the state treasury.

After the judgment was pronounced, both Shang Rongduo and Li Yuming refused to accept it and appealed to the Sichuan High People's Court.

Shang Rongduo's grounds of appeal: He, in accordance with the authorization of the College's administrative committee, used the RMB 200,000 to heavily reward those who made outstanding contributions in the enrollment work, which was a normal act of performing his duties; the distribution of RMB 57,000 as a reward for completing enrollment tasks was approved by the school's supervising leader and did not constitute embezzlement of public funds; of that amount, RMB 50,000 was used by him when giving red envelopes to relevant persons during New Year visits. These persons testified in denial only because they had an interest in this case, and thus the probative value of their denials is insufficient. He did not subjectively intend to illegally possess public property and thus did not constitute corruption.

Li Yuming's grounds of appeal: "Discretionary admission fees" are arbitrary charges explicitly prohibited by the state and are the school's illegal income; using this illegal income from students' parents to heavily reward those who contributed was a decision made by the College's administrative committee after study; therefore, distributing "discretionary admission fees" as bonuses only infringed upon the private property rights of the students' parents, not the ownership of state property, and did not constitute corruption. In addition, he had voluntarily surrendered and the first-instance court did not consider this.

The Sichuan High People's Court, after trial, confirmed the facts found in the first instance.

The Sichuan High People's Court held:

The state administrative authorities explicitly prohibit schools from collecting "discretionary admission fees" in enrollment work. The former College's administrative committee violated this prohibition by arbitrarily deciding to collect "discretionary admission fees" and deciding to use part of them to reward enrollment staff. This fact is true. The "discretionary admission fees" were fees illegally collected by the former College in its own name. Before the administrative authorities investigate and penalize the school's arbitrary charges, these fees should be regarded as public property managed by the Student Affairs Office under the authorization of the former College, i.e., public funds. The conduct of defendants Shang Rongduo, Li Yuming, and others in conspiring to intercept and embezzle these funds infringed upon the ownership of public property and constituted the crime of corruption.

The minutes of the College's administrative committee meeting on March 12, 2001, prove that the committee did form an opinion agreeing to use "discretionary admission fees" to appropriately reward those who performed outstandingly in the enrollment work when studying the reward method for the 2000 enrollment work. However, this opinion does not prove that defendants Shang Rongduo, Li Yuming, and others thereby acquired the right to conceal the actual income and expenditure of the "discretionary admission fees" and to privately distribute RMB 200,000 of them.

Defendant Li Yuming truthfully confessed to all the criminal facts only after the investigation authority had already uncovered all the leads of the case and interrogated him. In accordance with Article 67 of the Criminal Law, Li Yuming did not "voluntarily surrender" and therefore cannot be deemed to have voluntarily surrendered.

Apart from the above three points, the other grounds of appeal and defense arguments raised by defendants Shang Rongduo, Li Yuming, and their defense counsels are all untenable; the reasons have already been stated in the first-instance judgment.

In conclusion, the original judgment had correct findings of fact, appropriate sentencing, and lawful trial procedures. Accordingly, the Sichuan High People's Court rendered the following ruling on June 17, 2004:

The appeal is dismissed and the original judgment is sustained.
